newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Scrapped Russian nuclear sub sinking in Pacific.
newsitem.headline: Scrapped Russian nuclear sub sinking in Pacific.

text.p: A 1970s-vintage Russian nuclear submarine, taken out of service four years ago and stored offshore waiting to be scrapped, is sinking, officials said on Friday.
They denied reports that it had been holed and had sunk to a depth of up to 20 metres (60 feet) and insisted there was no radiation danger.
Radiation tests were being carried out every half hour and levels were normal so far, an official in the Far Eastern port of Petropavlovsk-Kamchatksky told Russian news agencies.
The emergencies ministry in Moscow said there was no danger, as the submarine's nuclear reactor had been removed and there were "no radioactive elements on board at all".
It denied reports that the submarine's hull had been damaged in a collision with another vessel as it was being moved.

"Nothing happened," a duty officer said by telephone. "Only the hull sank, and that only a little bit. There has been nothing inside for ages. It's like a tin can. The water started leaking inside and the vessel began to sink."

Itar-Tass and Interfax news agencies had said the submarine sank to a depth of 18-20 metres (55-60 feet). They said they had unconfirmed information that one or two sections had filled with water after a collision with another vessel.
Work was under way to raise the vessel by pumping in air.
An official from the emergencies ministry in Vladivostok on Russia's Pacific coast declined to give details of the incident.
"Nothing terrible happened. Radiation levels are normal. The vessel has been sitting there for four years waiting to be dismantled. There is no danger," he said by telephone.
Fleet commanders are very sensitive to reports that old nuclear submarines are being stored in dangerous conditions.

A former naval officer working for the Norwegian-based Bellona environmental organisation was arrested and charged with treason in 1996 after he wrote a report on the dangers posed by ageing nuclear submarines.
He was released after nearly a year in jail but the charges against him still stand.
Russia, struggling with a post-communist economic crisis, has few funds to scrap submarines taken out of service because of age or under international disarmament deals.
The worst accident involving a working submarine occurred in 1989, when fire broke out aboard the submarine Komsomolets.
The vessel sank, killing 42 crew members, and still lies under the sea off northern Norway. Bellona says it probably had two nuclear missiles on board.
